zh.q: 江河不断注入大海，为什么大海的水没有增多？
zh.concl: 大海的水没有增多，是因为支出的蒸发与收入的降水、河流回水正好相抵——蒸发的海水去了陆地上空，又以径流的形式回到海洋。
points: 教材给的半个答案：太阳加热海水使海水蒸发，河流注入大海补充蒸发的消耗，海水既不会增多也不会减少（p.46）。
完整的账在这里：海洋每年蒸发 1100 mm（示意），其中约 110 mm 的海洋当量由河流送回、990 mm 在海上直接降落，收支相抵。
蒸发的海水没有消失——它去了陆地上空，又顺着河流回来；世界里五个环节各占一处，指得出来。

zh.q: 水是从哪里变成水汽的？
zh.concl: 太阳辐射越强，海面蒸发越强；蒸发量一变，下游的输送、降水、径流全都跟着变。
points: 水汽从水面（和土面、植物）蒸发出来，动力是太阳辐射（教材「在太阳辐射作用下大量蒸发」）。
太阳辐射 1.00 → 1.40：海洋蒸发 1100 → 1540 mm/a（示意），海面水汽雾跟着变厚。
蒸发一变，输送、降水、径流三格同时变——五个环节是一条链，不是五个孤立的名词。

zh.q: 陆地上的水汽是从哪里来的？
zh.concl: 陆地上的水汽既来自地面、水面蒸发，也来自植物蒸腾；植被越密，蒸腾占比越大、下渗也更多。
points: 陆地上的水汽有两个来源：地面、水面（含湖面）蒸发与植物蒸腾（教材 p.47「地面、水面蒸发和植物蒸腾」）。
植被 40 % → 80 %：蒸腾 147 → 294、土面蒸发 343 → 196（蒸散总量 490 不变，只是分配变了）。
植被同时让下渗更多（根系），这是第 7 步砂田那条线的前奏。

zh.q: 水汽怎样从海洋上空跑到陆地上空？
zh.concl: 海洋的水汽被气流送到陆地上空，输送越强，陆地得到的降水越多、海上直接降落的越少。
points: 水汽被气流输送到大陆上空（教材 p.46「水汽上升到空中，被气流输送到大陆上空」）。
海洋的水是「借」给陆地的，借多少由输送决定——第 6 步要用这条线索解释大循环。

zh.q: 落到地面的水，怎样回到海洋？
zh.concl: 落到地面的水一部分蒸发蒸腾、一部分成为地表径流、一部分下渗成地下径流，后两者最后都回到海洋。
points: 降落到地面的水或被蒸发（蒸腾），或沿地面流动形成地表径流，或渗入地下形成地下径流（教材 p.47）。
陆地降水 759 = 蒸散 490 + 下渗 110 + 地表径流 159；下渗的水以地下径流 110 回到海洋。
下渗不是「漏掉」，是另一条回海的路——剖面里两支箭头的终点接得上。

zh.q: 三类循环，各走哪一条路？
zh.concl: 海陆间循环把海洋的水送到陆地、再经江河送回海洋，使陆地水不断得到补充；陆地内循环只有本地蒸发蒸腾与降水；海上内循环只在海上完成。
points: 三类循环按发生的空间范围分：海陆间循环（大循环）、陆地内循环、海上内循环（教材 p.46）。
拨档看：陆地内档里陆地仍下雨（490）但径流入海为 0；海上内档里陆地降水为 0；海陆间档里陆地降水全部来自海洋输送。
大循环使陆地上的水不断得到补充、水资源得以再生（p.46）——这正是本课主线问题的答案。

zh.q: 铺一层砂石，改的是哪几个环节？
zh.concl: 砂石覆盖层让这块田的下渗更多、土面蒸发更少，于是同一份降水里更多留在土里、更少流走——改的是蒸发与下渗两个环节，降水本身没有变。
points: 砂田是耕作土面上铺 10—15 厘米砂石覆盖层，作物成行种在砾石里（教材 p.48 活动、图 3.3）。
同一块田、同一份降水：铺上砾石后田块下渗 110 → 335、土面蒸发 343 → 172、地表径流 159 → 106（示意；曲线方向见图 3.4 / 3.5）。
改的是「蒸发」与「下渗」两个环节——省下的土面蒸发留在土里，所以地表径流也更少；陆地降水 759 与径流入海 269 这些全局读数不变，一块田的措施不会改全球收支。

zh.concl: 水循环维持全球水量的动态平衡、让水体不断更新，但更新周期相差上千倍，所以在一定时空范围内水资源是有限的；它同时是物质迁移与能量转换的过程。
points: 水循环使地球上各种水体处于不断更新状态，从而维持全球水量的动态平衡（教材 p.48）。
但更新周期差得极远：江河 16 天、湖泊 17 年、深层地下水 1400 年、高山冰川 1600 年、海洋 2500 年、极地冰川 9700 年（表 3.1）。
所以在一定时空范围内水资源是有限的：用水超过更新速度或水体被污染，就会短缺；径流还不断塑造地表、向海洋输送泥沙，是海陆联系的纽带（p.49）。

zh.q: 考核：让陆地径流入海 320 mm/a 以上、下渗 180 mm/a 以上
points: 达标条件是「陆地径流入海 ≥ 320 mm/a」且「田块下渗 ≥ 180 mm/a」：前一个由水汽输送管，后一个由地表覆盖（下渗比例）管。
参考工况径流入海 269、田块下渗 110；把输送拨到 14 % 并铺砂田即可达标（377 / 427）。
只拉输送也能过（30 % 时径流 808、田块下渗 331）——现实里「多来水」和「留住水」是两条不同思路，砂田属于后者。

en.q: Rivers keep flowing into the sea, so why doesn't the sea get fuller?
en.concl: The sea doesn't get fuller because the outflow by evaporation exactly balances the inflow by precipitation and river return; evaporated sea water goes to the sky over land and returns to the ocean as runoff.
points: The textbook's half-answer: the sun heats sea water and it evaporates, rivers flow into the sea to make up for evaporation, and the sea neither grows nor shrinks (p.46).
The full account is here: the ocean evaporates 1100 mm a year (schematic), of which about 110 mm ocean-equivalent comes back via rivers and 990 mm falls directly on the sea, so the budget balances.
Evaporated sea water doesn't vanish; it goes to the sky over land and comes back down the rivers; each of the five links has its own place in the scene and can be pointed to.

en.q: Where does water turn into water vapor?
en.concl: The stronger the solar radiation, the more the sea evaporates; when evaporation changes, transport, precipitation and runoff downstream all follow.
points: Water vapor evaporates from water surfaces (and soil and plants), driven by solar radiation (textbook: "evaporates in large amounts under solar radiation").
Solar radiation 1.00 → 1.40: ocean evaporation 1100 → 1540 mm/a (schematic), and the vapor haze over the sea thickens with it.
Change evaporation and transport, precipitation and runoff all change together; the five links are one chain, not five isolated terms.

en.q: Where does water vapor over land come from?
en.concl: Water vapor on land comes both from evaporation off ground and water surfaces and from plant transpiration; the denser the vegetation, the larger the share of transpiration and the more infiltration.
points: Water vapor on land has two sources: evaporation from ground and water surfaces (including lakes), and plant transpiration (textbook p.47 "evaporation from ground and water surfaces and plant transpiration").
Vegetation 40 % → 80 %: transpiration 147 → 294, soil evaporation 343 → 196 (total evapotranspiration 490 unchanged, only the split changes).
Vegetation also increases infiltration (through roots), a prelude to the gravel-field thread in step 7.

en.q: How does water vapor get from over the ocean to over the land?
en.concl: Ocean water vapor is carried over land by air currents; the stronger the transport, the more rain the land gets and the less falls directly on the sea.
points: Water vapor is carried by air currents to over the continent (textbook p.46 "water vapor rises into the air and is carried by air currents to over the continent").
Transport 10 % → 20 %: land precipitation 759 → 1029, ocean precipitation 990 → 880, surface runoff 159 → 318 (schematic).
The ocean's water is "lent" to the land, and how much is set by transport; step 6 uses this thread to explain the major cycle.

en.q: How does water that falls on the ground get back to the ocean?
en.concl: Of the water falling on the ground, some evaporates or transpires, some becomes surface runoff, and some infiltrates to become groundwater flow; the last two both end up back in the ocean.
points: Water falling on the ground either evaporates (or transpires), flows over the surface as surface runoff, or soaks in to become groundwater flow (textbook p.47).
Land precipitation 759 = evapotranspiration 490 + infiltration 110 + surface runoff 159; infiltrated water returns to the ocean as groundwater flow of 110.
Infiltration isn't "leaking away"; it's another road back to the sea; the ends of the two arrows in the cross-section connect.

en.q: Three types of cycle: which path does each take?
en.concl: The sea–land cycle sends ocean water to land and back to the ocean through rivers, constantly replenishing water on land; the inland cycle has only local evapotranspiration and precipitation; the ocean cycle is completed entirely over the sea.
points: The three types of cycle are classified by spatial extent: the sea–land cycle (major cycle), the inland cycle and the ocean cycle (textbook p.46).

Switch through them: in the inland setting it still rains on land (490) but runoff to sea is 0; in the ocean setting land precipitation is 0; in the sea–land setting all land precipitation comes from ocean transport.
The major cycle keeps replenishing water on land so water resources are renewed (p.46); that's the answer to this lesson's main question.

en.q: Lay down a gravel layer: which links does it change?
en.concl: The gravel layer gives this plot more infiltration and less soil evaporation, so more of the same rainfall stays in the soil and less runs off; it changes the evaporation and infiltration links, while the precipitation itself doesn't change.
points: A gravel field has a 10–15 cm layer of sand and gravel laid over the tilled soil, with crops planted in rows in the gravel (textbook p.48 activity, Fig. 3.3).
Same plot, same rainfall: with gravel, plot infiltration goes 110 → 335, soil evaporation 343 → 172, surface runoff 159 → 106 (schematic; curve directions in Figs. 3.4 / 3.5).

It changes the "evaporation" and "infiltration" links: the soil evaporation saved stays in the soil, so surface runoff is also lower; global readings such as land precipitation 759 and runoff to sea 269 don't change, since one field's measures don't change the global budget.

en.q: Why are water resources said to be "limited"?
en.concl: The water cycle maintains the dynamic balance of global water and keeps water bodies renewing, but renewal periods differ by thousands of times, so within a given time and place water resources are limited; it is also a process of material transfer and energy conversion.
points: The water cycle keeps Earth's water bodies constantly renewing, maintaining the dynamic balance of global water (textbook p.48).
But renewal periods differ enormously: rivers 16 days, lakes 17 years, deep groundwater 1400 years, mountain glaciers 1600 years, ocean 2500 years, polar ice 9700 years (Table 3.1).

So within a given time and place water resources are limited: using water faster than it renews, or polluting it, causes shortages; runoff also keeps shaping the land and carrying sediment to the sea, linking sea and land (p.49).

en.q: Assessment: get land runoff to sea above 320 mm/a and infiltration above 180 mm/a
points: The pass conditions are "land runoff to sea ≥ 320 mm/a" and "plot infiltration ≥ 180 mm/a": the first is controlled by vapor transport, the second by ground cover (infiltration ratio).
The reference case has runoff to sea 269 and plot infiltration 110; setting transport to 14 % and laying a gravel field passes (377 / 427).

Pulling transport alone also passes (at 30 %, runoff 808 and plot infiltration 331); in reality "bring in more water" and "keep the water" are two different approaches, and gravel fields belong to the second.
